label: ReFED
raw:
ReFED
Supporting Resources & Services
ReFED is a national nonprofit working across the food system to reduce food loss and waste. ReFED gathers data about food waste, serving as the definitive source for data and economic analysis about food waste, the solutions to fight it, and accessible methods for tracking progress. ReFED also works with businesses and community organizations to reduce food waste, build networks, and influence policy. Finally, ReFED funds solutions through its 'Catalytic Grant Fund'. The Catalytic Grant Fund is designed to accelerate the development and implementation of food waste solutions across the full food system by providing non-recoverable and recoverable grants and post-grant support to initiatives with high impact potential as measured by food waste reduced and GHG emissions reduced. The Catalytic Grant Fund deploys its capital through an ongoing series of open call cycles that are built around specific, priority food waste themes. See their open calls here: https://grantfund.refed.org/ Retaaza, a local Atlanta business dedicated to paying farmers and rescuring surplus food, was awarded from this fund in 2025 to reduce harvest losses on Georgia farms.
Funding | Advocacy
Nonprofit
info@refed.org

label: Big Bethel AME Church
description: Big Bethel African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church traces its roots back to 1847, with a group of enslaved persons who were part of "Union Church," the very first congregation formed in Atlanta. Although Union Church, which eventually disbanded, was established for whites, the original enslaved group that was allowed to worship there remained intact. Whites eventually granted a petition for those enslaved to have their own church and set aside $700 for that purpose. In 1855, "Bethel Tabernacle" was completed. Indeed, while Big Bethel is often referred to as Atlanta's first Black congregation, it is more accurately recognized as Atlanta's oldest congregation, Black or white.
